2 Abstract One of the best options to utilize CO2 is to convert it to useful chemicals, which may lead to economic and environmental benefits. In the present work, highly stable metallic copper nanoparticles (Cu NPs) have been synthesized and characterized by different physio-chemical characterization techniques like X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), Brunauer-EmmetTeller (BET), etc. The prepared Cu NPs exhibit porous morphology in pure metallic state with high surface area of 630 m2.g-1. From electrochemical experiments, total Faradaic efficiency (FE) for the liquid products reached to ∼58 % at -0.8 V (vs. RHE) using prepared Cu NPs as an electrocatalyst. The Cu NPs majorly produced formic acid (2.3 mM) with small quantities of acetic acid (13 µM), ethanol (51 µM), and n-propanol (32 µM) under studied conditions. In addition, FE for formic acid remained constant around ∼40% at − 0.8 V vs. RHE) when reusing the same electrode number of times. The good performance of Cu NPs might be due to the presence of lots of micropores on the surface, which increases CO2 adsorption for its conversion to chemicals. Keywords Copper nanoparticles; CO2 reduction; nanoporous Cu electrode; Faradaic efficiency

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Naturally available fuels (crude oil, coal, etc.) are used as the world’s primary source of energy [1]. The utilization of naturally available fuel is drastically increasing to fulfill the world's energy demand due to rapid rise in population and its low cost. Fossil fuel accounts for more than 85 % usage for energy generation [2]. Therefore, the atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration has been increasing drastically [3]. This increase in the concentration of CO2 is a very sincere concern as it creates high impact on global climate
3 change. In addition, increasing the CO2 concentration in the atmosphere is resulting in ocean acidification and influencing the growth of many aquatic species present in the ocean [4]. The atmospheric CO2 could be reduced by converting it into useful chemicals using electrochemical reduction of CO2 (ECO2R) driven by renewable energy. Several metal complexes [5-8], pure metals [9], polymer [10], alloys [11-14] and metal free [15, 16] electrocatalysts have been studied for ECO2R . However, different electrocatalytic properties were shown by various metal electrodes to produce different chemicals. The copper has a unique ability to reduce CO2 to many products like methanol, ethanol, propanol [17], formic acid/formate (depending on pH), etc. which are relatively value-added commodity chemicals. Therefore, there is great interest in studying Cu to improve product selectivity for maximizing economic and environmental benefits (see Supporting Information, SI-1). To date, different Cu based electrocatalysts have been investigated to improve the selectivity and activity, including the exposed surface facets [18], particle size [19], the control of macrostructure [20], and bimetallic alloys formation with the use of secondary metals [21]. High overpotential and poor selectivity due to the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) remains a huge challenge for selective ECO2R [22]. Therefore, recent investigations have focused on suppressing HER and improving carbonaceous product selectivity. The use of copper electrode for ECO2R is extensively studied by many researchers [9, 23-31]. The very first report was available in 1989 by Hori et al. [25], where the authors studied Cu in the aqueous inorganic electrolyte and observed CO, CH4, C2H4, C2H5OH, and C3H7OH at ambient conditions. Recently, cuprous oxide (Cu2O) derived copper nanoparticles was reported by Kas et al. [26] for ECO2R. From their online electrochemical mass spectroscopy study, they reported that all ECO2R actually proceeds on the newly formed metallic copper particles (in-situ) and not on as-deposited Cu2O. Formic acid with 22 % FE
4 was observed in the liquid phase. Two separate studies were carried out by Frese et al. [27] and Le et al. [5] on the effect of different pretreatment methods on Cu foils. Both have reported methanol as the main product with the highest production rate on Cu2O films deposited on stainless steel substrate and Cu deposited on titanium foil pretreated in the air at 500 oC, which is higher than that of anodized and annealed Cu in air. Griffin et al. [28] reported Cu2O nanoparticles coated on a glassy carbon electrode was used for ECO2R, which resulted in the production of the C1-C2 hydrocarbons (CH4 and C2H4), CO, H2, and multicarbon alcohols (C2H5OH, 1-C3H7OH). They also studied physio-chemical properties of used catalyst by SEM and XRD and reported that, during CO2 reduction, the fractional conversion of the Cu2O to Cu0 takes place. Thus, there might be a critical role of Cu0 species in the ECO2R. In 2011, Li et al. [29] synthesized Cu2O layer on the copper foil and then reduced it back to metallic copper during ECO2R. It was reported that the metallic copper produced by the Cu2O reduction was more active towards the ECO2R to formate ions and shown higher current densities than polycrystalline copper foil. Chi et al. [30] synthesized different CuO nanoparticles of different morphologies and reported 36.1 % FE for ethanol at -1.7 V after in situ reduction to metallic Cu. Tan et al. [32] reported high surface area Cu2O@Cu-MOF for production of CH4 and C2H4, and also observed the appearance of Cu0 phase after ECO2R. The literature study suggests that the reduction of cupric oxides/cuprous oxides to copper takes place in the initial phase of ECO2R (within a few minutes) of applying the electrode potential. Thus, the actual ECO2R occurs on metallic copper and not on its oxides [31]. Therefore, in this work, citrate stabilized metallic Cu nanoparticles (Cu NPs) were prepared and coated on a porous carbon paper (Cu NPs/carbon paper), to be used as a working electrode for ECO2R in CO2 saturated aqueous 0.1 M KHCO3 solution. The effect of key governing parameters like electrolysis potential was explored to obtain the optimal
5 electrolysis condition. Effects of potential on the final product concentration, production rates, and Faradaic efficiency (i.e. selectivity) were studied. Kinetics is studied by Tafel analysis and dependence of CO2 partial pressure on product generation is also explored. Moreover, reusability of the electrode at optimized conditions is also discussed. The performance of the Cu NPs was compared with that of commercial Cu foil

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
sections.text: Cupric chloride dihydrate (99.9%) (CuCl2.2H2O), Cu foil (99.7%, approx. 0.1 mm thickness), hydrazine hydrate (80%) (N2H4.H2O), and trisodium citrate dihydrate (99%) (C6H5Na3O7.2H2O) were purchased from Loba Chemie, India. Potassium bicarbonate (99.99 %) (KHCO3), Nafion dispersion solution (5 wt. %), isopropanol (IPA), sulfuric acid (99.99 %) (H2SO4) were procured from Sigma-Aldrich. Porous carbon paper (approx. 0.18 mm thickness and 77 % porosity) was purchased from CeTech Japan. All the aqueous solutions were prepared in double-distilled water. Analytical grade chemicals were used during the experiments without any further purification.

sections.heading: 2.2.1. Synthesis of Cu nanoparticles
sections.text:
Citrate stabilized metallic copper nanoparticles were synthesized using the method reported by Chatterjee et al. [33]. In brief, 60 mL of double-distilled water was taken in 500 mL of round bottomed flask and 10 g of cupric chloride dihydrate was dissolved in it. The color of the solution changed to royal blue, indicating the formation of hexaaquacopper(II) complex ions. Subsequently, about 10 g of trisodium citrate dihydrate was mixed to the above solution. Then, the temperature of this precursor solution was raised to 60 oC. Hydrazine
6 hydrate was heated separately to 60 oC, and 20 mL of this was added in the Cu precursor solution (at once) under vigorous stirring. After this, the solution turned to dark brown signifying the reduction of CuCl2.2H2O to metallic Cu. Stirring was continued for another 20 min and then the temperature was lowered down to 25 oC. Obtained copper solution was kept undisturbed for overnight at room temperature. During this step, suspended Cu NPs slowly settled at the bottom and clear solution was obtained in supernatant. The settled material was thoroughly washed with water and subsequently with ethanol then it was dried in vacuum oven for 15 h at 50 oC. Fine powder was obtained by crushing dried nanopowder in a mortarpestle. Schematic of synthesis of citrate stabilized Cu NPs is given in Fig. S2.

sections.heading: 2.2.2. Preparation of electrodes
sections.text: Surface preparation of purchased carbon paper was carried out to remove dust so that electrochemical activity could truly be attributed to the Cu NPs. For this, the carbon paper was cut into 2 cm x 2 cm dimensions. These pieces were ultrasonically treated in pure acetone for 5 min. and then the carbon paper was properly dried at 105 oC for 2 h. The mixture of 8±0.2 mg of the Cu NPs, 1 mL of IPA and 50 μL Nafion® (5 wt. % solution) was sonicated for 30 min in a 2 mL vial to obtain homogeneous catalyst ink. Obtained suspension ink was dropped on to a pretreated carbon paper and dried under the incandescent lamp. This acts as a working electrode (WE) and represented as Cu NPs/carbon paper in further discussion.

sections.heading: 2.3. Characterization of synthesized nanoparticles
sections.text:
X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed using a PAN analytical X-Pert PRO diffractometer (equipped with Cu-Kα radiation, λ = 1.54 Å) over a range of 20 < 2 < 80o. The permanent porosity and surface area was measured using a Micromeritics ASAP 2010 sorption analyzer using Brunauer-Emmet-Teller (BET) method. Prior to sorption study, the sample was degassed at 220 oC under vacuum for 6 h to remove any adsorbed gases from
7 surface of the sample. Morphological features of Cu NPs were analyzed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) using a JEOL JSM-6510 LV instrument operated at 20 kV and JEOL JEM 21000 operated at 200 kV respectively. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectra were recorded on a FTIR spectrometer (Perkin Elmer Spectrum 100 FTIR) in the range of 4000–400 cm-1 wavelength. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed on Kratos Axis Ultra DLD system (equipped with a monochromatic Al-Kα source operated at anode potential of 15 kV). The hydrodynamic size distribution of synthesized nanoparticles was determined on Brookhaven 90 plus particle size analyzer. The measured autocorrelation function is determined on MAS OPTION software by fitting the data in a lognormal particle size distribution function. From the best fit, the hydrodynamic size was determined.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical CO2 reduction measurements
sections.text:
The ECO2R experiments were performed using a “Wave Driver 20” Bi-potentiostat (Pine Instruments, USA) with a three-electrode system in customized H-type cell as shown in Fig. S3. Anode and cathode compartments were separated by Nafion 117 membrane to avoid the oxidation of products at the anode surface. Standard Ag/AgCl (saturated with KCl) and Cu NPs/carbon paper were used as a reference electrode (RE) and working electrode (WE) respectively, which were kept in the same compartment. Distance between RE and WE were kept minimum (0.5 mm) to minimize uncompensated solution resistance [34]. Pt foil was used as a counter electrode. All the ECO2R experiments were performed at 25 oC and 1 atm. The cyclic voltammetry (CV) studies were performed in a high purity N2 as well as CO2 saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte solution. The double layer capacitance measurement was performed using CO2 saturated 0.1 M KHCO3. The controlled-potential electrolysis was conducted in 60 mL high purity CO2 saturated aqueous 0.1 M KHCO3 (pH=6.8) electrolyte
8 solution in each compartment. The study for CO2 partial pressure dependence was carried out under CO2 partial pressure ranging from 0.1 to 1.0 atm. A mixture of N2 and CO2 gases in a desired proportion was used to purge the cathodic compartment at least 20 minutes before electrolysis and maintained a flow rate of 20 mL min-1 during electrolysis. A freshly prepared electrode was used for electrolysis at each data point and the formate partial current densities were measured at -0.8 V vs. RHE. All the potentials are reported against standard reverse hydrogen electrode (RHE) and converted by using the following equation. (1)pHVV AgClAgmeasuredvsRHEvs *059.0197.0/..

sections.heading: 2.5 Product analysis and calculations
sections.text:
Quantitative and qualitative analysis of the liquid products produced during ECO2R was performed (without any further treatment) using high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) (Agilent Technologies, Germany 1260 Infinity II series). After every experiment, samples were collected from the reactor and analyzed with HPLC. Sample vials were placed in a low temperature environment (10 oC) before injection and 100 μL of each sample was injected through a 0.22 µm Nylon syringe filter. Hi-Plex H column (Agilent Technologies, Part No- PL1170-68730) was used for product separation. The column oven was kept at a constant temperature of 60 oC with a flow rate of 0.6 mL.min-1 of 1 mM H2SO4 prepared in HPLC grade water (S. D. Fine-Chem Limited, India) as eluent. For identifying the product concentration in the sample, the effluent stream exiting the column was passed through a refractive index detector (Agilent Technologies, Part No- G71628). HPLC system was conditioned along with a column for 6 h before analysis. A standard calibration curve was drawn by analyzing the known concentration (20, 100, 1000 and 5000 µmol.L-1) of formic acid, acetic acid, methanol, ethanol, and n-propanol prepared in CO2 saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution. The product concentration in the sample was calculated using the calibration curve.
9 After the analysis, the column was cleaned for 1 h by passing 1mM H2SO4. In addition to HPLC, 1H NMR analysis was used to confirm the different liquid products formation and quantification (see Supporting Information, SI-2). In this research work, only liquid products were taken in account. The Faradaic efficiency for obtained products was calculated by using equation (2). sections.heading: 3.1. Physico-chemical characterization
sections.text:
The XRD pattern of citrate stabilized Cu NPs recorded from a powder sample, reflects three diffraction characteristic peaks at 2 of 43.3o, 50.4o, 74.1o which are assigned to (220), (200), and (111) planes of Cu cubic crystal respectively [JCPDS card no. 01-085-1326] as shown in Fig. 1a. They also exhibit small peaks at 2θ = 35.75° and 38.9° associated with the presence of CuO phase [JCPDS card no. 01-089-5899]. XPS was used to study the oxidation state of copper. It shows the two strong peaks at 951.4 eV and 931 eV, which correspond to Cu 2p1/2 and Cu 2p3/2 core levels respectively, confirming the metallic structure of the Cu nanoparticles [35]. The deconvoluted XPS spectrum is shown in Fig. 1b. Small satellite peak at 945.5 eV [36] was also observed suggesting that Cu NPs contains oxide (at least on the surface) in minor proportion. The XRD
10
also indicated the presence of CuO in the sample. It is important to note that because nanosized Cu can be readily oxidized by O2, it is possible that the observed CuO phase was formed during sample handling in air following in situ reduction [37]..
Fig. 1 a) XRD patterns and b) High-resolution XPS spectrum recorded for citrate stabilized Cu NPs
Morphology and dispersion of nanoparticles greatly affect the electrode performance
and selectivity [38]. Fig. 2a shows HR-TEM image of citrate stabilized Cu NPs together with their selected area electron diffraction patterns. The particles are observed to be nanostructured. The mean diameter of the Cu NPs is 20-30 nm. Large aggregates are observed due to the separation of Cu NPs from solvent. Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) image shows that Cu NPs are highly crystalline in nature with (111), (200) and (220) cubic planes of metallic Cu. EDX analysis shows all the peaks are related to the chemical composition of nanoparticles and substrate, made of Cu, C, and O as shown in Fig. 2c. The elemental analysis of the sample confirmed the formation of 99 wt. % pure Cu NPs, which is in good accord with the results of XRD and XPS.

The saturation concentration of CO2 in 0.1 M KHCO3 (≈ 35 mM) [41]) leads to a downward shift of the CD curves suggesting the ECO2R activity along with HER [42].

The surface roughness factor of the as-prepared working electrode after reduction was
estimated based on the double layer capacitance (Cdl). Cdl measurements were performed using CO2 saturated 0.1 M KHCO3, CV were taken between 0.30 and 0.50 V vs. RHE at various scan rates as shown in Fig. S6. It can be seen that Cu NPs/carbon paper has the Cdl of 1.17 mF.cm-2, which is much larger than that of bare carbon support i.e. 38 µF.cm-2, suggesting its largest effective electrochemical active surface area for reduction of CO2. Further, to estimate the surface roughness factor, the capacitance value of bare carbon paper
14
support was subtracted from the capacitance value measured for Cu NPs/carbon paper, and divided by 0.036 mF.cm-2 (reported capacitance value for electropolished copper foil) [43]. High roughness factor of 31.44 indicates that prepared electrode has more active sites for reduction of CO2.

sections.heading: 3.2.3 Controlled-potential electrolysis
sections.text:
Since CO2 reduction and water splitting both are occurring at applied potentials
during full CV study, it cannot give direct proof for any specific type of reaction occurring on the cathode surface. Therefore, controlled-potential electrolysis (CPE) was studied in a range from - 0.4 to -1.2 V (vs. RHE) for 2 h in CO2 saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution with continuous CO2 supply to produce the CO2 reduction products. Fig. 4b shows the current density normalized by geometric area versus time data for different applied potentials. It can be seen that a rapid decrease in current density from very high to a low value was observed at initial stage and further, it got stabilized. No product was observed (as per HPLC analysis) during this period, which indicates that all of the charge supplied was consumed for the electrocatalyst reduction itself. At high applied potentials (> -0.9 V vs. RHE), disturbance in recorded current was observed probably due to a high rate of hydrogen evolution or formation of other gaseous products which form gas bubbles at electrode surface as shown in Fig. S7.
Chromatogram of a standard mixture containing 5 mM.L-1 each of formic acid, acetic
acid, methanol, ethanol, and n-propanol is displayed in Fig. S8a. This shows that all the peaks are well resolved. The electrolyte peak (negative) obtained at a retention time of 24 min was also observed in all the HPLC chromatograms, including the blank CO2 saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte solution, which was not considered for calculations. The corresponding standard calibration plot was drawn by analyzing known concentrations of
15
formic acid, acetic acid, methanol, ethanol, n-propanol and iso-propanol mixture prepared in CO2 saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 as shown in Fig. S8b.
As shown in Fig. S9, different peaks were obtained at a retention time of 16, 18, 26
and 34 min corresponding to formic acid, acetic acid, ethanol and n-propanol respectively. At all the studied conditions, a mixture of reduction product with different selectivity was obtained, similar to reported in previous literature [9, 30, 44]. Moles of individual products produced were quantified using the calibration plot, and the Faradaic efficiency was calculated by using equation (2). To verify the liquid products derived from dissolved CO2, the electrocatalytic experiment was performed in N2 saturated KHCO3 solution (without CO2 purging) at -0.8 V vs. RHE. No peaks were observed in HPLC analysis (see Fig. S9) after electrochemical reduction for 2 h, indicating all liquid products were coming from CO2 rather than from the reduction of functional groups (i.e. HCO3-, COO-, CO-) present in stabilizing material of Cu NPs or electrolyte.

sections.heading: 3.3 Products vs. potential
sections.text:
Fig. 5 displays the concentrations of products, obtained after 2 h of reaction time at different electrode potentials, which are divided into two groups viz., major and minor products. Formic acid was identified as the major reaction product. At lowest applied potential (-0.4 V vs. RHE), the formic acid/fomate concentration was about 58 µM. It was increasing with increasing applied potential up to -0.9 V (vs. RHE) where a maximum formic acid concentration of 2.91 mM was observed and it decreased to 1.10 mM with further increase in applied potential to -1.2 V (vs. RHE). Similar trend was observed for other minor products. The minimum concentration of ethanol, n-propanol and acetic acid was detected at -0.8, -0.7 and -0.6 V (vs. RHE), respectively. The final concentration of all these products increased with an increase in applied potential from -0.6 to -1.0 V (vs. RHE), and a further increase in applied potential, resulted in decreased concentration. This may be due to the
16
limited availability of CO2 in CO2 saturated aqueous 0.1 M KHCO3 and the formation of gaseous products at such a high negative potential greatly restricts the formation of more complex multi-carbon liquid products in higher concentrations.

As shown in Fig. 6, formic acid formation rates at Cu NPs/carbon paper electrode are
quite high ranging from 29 to 1460 µmol.L-1.h-1 as compared to other products. Acetic acid yield ranged from 6 to 10 µmol.L-1.h-1, ethanol yield ranged from 16 to 67 µmol.L-1.h-1; and n-propanol yields from 16 to 26 µmol.L-1.h-1. Formation rates of products typically increased with potential from –0.4 V (vs. RHE) and reached a maxima near - 0.9 V (vs. RHE), then decreased significantly at potentials more cathodic than - 0.9 V (vs. RHE) along with enhanced gas bubble formation at electrode surface probably due to hydrogen evolution or gaseous product generation.

sections.heading: 3.4 Mechanistic analysis
sections.text:
The mechanistic insight on a Cu NPs and flat Cu foil was studied by Tafel analysis
using partial current density of formate in 0.1 M KHCO3 solution. Tafel slope of Cu NPs and flat Cu foil was found to be 154 mV dec-1 and 206 mV dec-1 respectively (Fig. S11). Decrease in the Tafel slope of Cu NPs compared to flat Cu foil further demonstrates the inherently improved efficiency of Cu NPs [46]. It is also observed that, at higher overpotentials, Tafel slope has increased indicating the effect of another rate-limiting step. In this case, the other consideration is most likely mass transport problems concerning the diffusion of products and reactants from / in the nanopores [48]. More experiments were conducted to provide further insight into the mechanism for reducing CO2 on Cu NPs. The dependence of CO2 reduction activity on CO2 partial pressure was investigated from 0.1 to 1 atm, which shows an approximate first-order dependence on the concentration of CO2 in the electrolyte (Fig. S12).
At lowest onset potential, only fomate was observed which required two electrons.
However, at higher overpotentials, more reduced products were observed as shown in Fig. 5. This suggests that, formate is generated with lowest kinetic barrier. Further, generation of C2C3 products have higher kinetic barriers [9], and are generated at higher overpotential. As stated earlier, similar trend was observed for C2 and C3 product generation. For multi carbon products, sufficient surface coverage and favorable reaction energies are required [17]. C-C coupling rate was initially increased with increasing overpotential and decreased with further increase in overpotential. This can be due to the mass transport problems as explained in previous paragraph. There are many possible explanations on reaction mechanism of different products. Based on some reports, *CO intermediates are more strongly bound on the Cu surface and converted into alcohols or hydrocarbons by *CO dimerization [25, 49]. It is also assumed that *CO dimerization is the key step in the selective reduction of *CO intermediates to *C2O2 or formyl species (*CHO) to produce alcohols on copper electrodes
20
[50]. The different reaction pathways of Cu-based electrocatalysts and their corresponding main products (including CO, CH4, C2H4, alcohols, and so on) are illustrated in Fig. S13. Here, * denotes a catalytic active site.

sections.heading: 3.5 Reusability study
sections.text:
Furthermore, after electrolysis, the reusability of the working electrode was also
studied. It is worth noting that it could be easily washed with water and then reused for next reaction run under the same conditions. The Faradaic efficiency of formate/formic acid could be maintained around 40±5 % for at least ten runs of repeated electrolysis at − 0.8 V (vs. RHE) as presented in Fig. 8a, but the total FE of acetic acid, ethanol, and n-propanol reduced from 23% to about 5 %. The electrocatalytic activity of copper for C2 products decreased significantly with the deposition of poisoning species (i.e. graphitic carbon) on the electrode surface as reported by Bard et al. [51] and other investigators [50, 52]. Also, metallic impurities from electrolyte solution can be adsorbed on catalyst surface due to a higher rate of OH− production (or H+ consumption) and K+ transfer into the catholyte at higher current densities. This is supported by appearance of K signal in EDX analysis after 20 h of ECO2R (Fig. S14). Hydrogen evolution continued at this very negative potential on the poisoned surface, but CO2 reduction to products, which requires active Cu surface, decreased. Long term performance of Cu NPs was also tested at constant cathode potential of −0.8 V (vs. RHE) for 20 h. The current density was kept a steady value at around 2.5 mA.cm-2 throughout the duration of the test (Fig. 8b). A slight disturbance in CD was observed due to minor fluctuations in CO2 flow rate.
To further study the morphology and phase of electrocatalyst after the CO2
electroreduction reaction for 20 h, post characterizations like SEM and XRD have been carried out, and the corresponding results are shown in Figs. S14 and S15. Before ECO2R,
21
the characteristic peaks at 2 of 43.3o, 50.4 o, 74.1o are assigned to (220), (200), and (111)
planes of Cu cubic crystal respectively [JCPDS card no. 01-085-1326]. Two small peaks at 35.7 o and 38.4 o are assigned to oxidized CuO and Cu2O species, respectively, indicating that the minor amount of Cu+ and Cu2+ phase is also present in Cu NPs. After the ECO2R, the initial small peaks at 35.7 o and 38.4 o of Cu2+ and Cu+ species disappeared due to the electrochemical reduction. The metallic Cu remained in cubic crystal shape after long term performance for 20 h ECO2R, indicating the relative stability of the as-made Cu NPs. Furthermore, no apparent changes were observed in morphology (Fig. S14), implying the good stability of the Cu NPs.

4. Conclusions
Copper nanoparticles having a high surface area (630 m2.g-1) and total pore volume of
0.528 cm3.g-1 with micropore volume of 0.062 cm3.g-1 have been synthesized and found to be in pure metallic state. The electrocatalytic properties of the nanoparticles towards CO2 reduction to chemicals in aqueous electrolyte have been studied. The synthesized nanoparticles show electrocatalytic reduction activity towards formate/formic acid, acetate, ethanol and n-propanol formation after coating on the carbon paper. In 2 h ECO2R, total
22
∼58% FE is observed for the liquid products. The favorable electrode potential is fund to be - 0.8 V (vs RHE) and at this potential, the concentration of formic acid/formate, acetic acid, ethanol and n-propanol are about 2.35, 0.013, 0.050 and 0.032 mM respectively. It is believed that nanoporous Cu NPs have great potential in developing efficient and green routes for ECO2R to produce useful chemicals and fuels.
